Where it began

Venkatesh Prasad was born in Bengaluru on 5 August 1969, and Kannada is his mother tongue. He studied as well as bowled: he took a Bachelor of Engineering at MSRIT and later a postgraduate certificate from the University of London.

He played his domestic cricket for Karnataka and was part of two Ranji Trophy-winning sides there.

The player

Prasad was a right-arm medium-fast bowler, and his partnership with Javagal Srinath was a feature of India's attack. He played 33 Tests between 1996 and 2001 and took 96 wickets at 35.00, with seven five-wicket innings and a best of 6 for 33.

Those best figures came against Pakistan in Chennai in 1999, on a pitch that offered him almost nothing, and included a spell of five wickets for no runs at all. In December 1996 he took ten wickets in a Test in Durban, and he also collected five-wicket hauls in England in 1996, the West Indies in 1997 and Sri Lanka in 2001. He played 161 one-day internationals as well, taking 196 wickets, and was part of the squad that reached the final of the 2000 ICC Champions Trophy.

What made him special

His great weapon was the slow leg-cutter. He was one of the first bowlers in the world to make it a regular part of his game, and it became his trademark. He liked a pitch with some help in it, but he could make his own luck when there was none.

At the 1996 World Cup, against Pakistan, he was struck for four and answered by bowling the batsman with the very next ball, a turning point in a match India went on to win. With the bat he was rather less fearsome: 203 Test runs at 7.52. Then again, he was not out in 20 of his 47 innings, so bowlers did not find him easy to shift.

Away from the middle

The CEAT International Cricketer of the Year award came his way for the 1996/97 season, and India gave him the Arjuna Award in 2000. After retiring in May 2005 he turned to coaching. He took the India Under-19 side to the final of the 2006 Under-19 World Cup, was India's bowling coach from 2007 to 2009, coached Royal Challengers Bangalore in their first season in 2008, and was bowling coach of Kings XI Punjab in 2018.

He also worked as a Kannada commentator and as a General Manager at Canara Bank, and in December 2025 he became President of the Karnataka State Cricket Association.

And finally

Five wickets for no runs is the sort of spell bowlers dream about and batsmen try to forget. Prasad managed it on a slow Chennai pitch, which tells you most of what you need to know about the leg-cutter.
